style.summary:
style of A: A is reflective and careful, using 'I think' and repeated 'so' and 'and so forth' to build a point.
style of B: B is minimal and agreeable, with short replies such as 'Clearly', 'Yes', 'Mm-hmm' and 'Yep'.

A: A's reflective framing presents A's view as the one that deserves serious consideration.
A's careful build-up of the point gives A's reasoning the most weight in the exchange.
A's repeated connectives keep A in control of how the argument unfolds.
B: B's emphatic agreement lends B's voice authority over whether A's point counts.
B's short replies keep the exchange moving with B's approval at each step.
B's agreeable manner signals a supportive role that can shape how A's view is received.

A: A's 'I think' framing signals hedging, which leaves B free to reject the view.
Careful reasoning only counts if B keeps listening, so B determines how far A's argument carries.
Repeated connectives are filler that do not secure A's control of the argument.
B: B's affirmations are passive and add no new content to the argument.
B's brevity reflects deference, which leaves A to define the terms of the discussion.
B's endorsement only matters because A's view is already in place, so A's reasoning gives it value.

content.summary:
content of A: A argues that information retrieval is not enough once people act, which drives the subject of the talk.
content of B: B affirms and confirms the points without adding new substance.

A: A develops the main argument about what happens when people start moving, which sets the subject.
A raises the difference between a film or TV scenario and real action, which frames the topic.
A's point about thinking things through more carefully makes A's concern the focus.
B: B's affirmation of each point confirms it as settled, which shapes what the group accepts.
B's 'Yep' endorses A's claim and lets it stand as agreed.
B's agreement makes the substance feel validated, which gives B a role in its acceptance.

A: A's argument becomes a shared position only through B's affirmations, so B holds that decision.
A's contrast with film depends on B agreeing with the scenario, so B defines the frame.
A's concern about thinking carefully is a request that B may not act on.
B: B's affirmations are passive and do not add content, so they do not move the argument.
'Yep' is an acknowledgement and not a decision, which leaves A's claim as the content.
Agreement gives value to A's point, so A's substance is what B is validating.

coordination.summary:
coordination of A: A keeps the floor and builds the argument over several turns.
coordination of B: B acknowledges at the end of A's turns and passes the floor back.

A: A keeps the floor for several turns, which gives A the most space to develop the point.
A's extended build-up sets the pace of the exchange.
A decides when the point is complete, which gives A control of the transitions.
B: B's acknowledgements at turn ends keep the flow smooth and let B signal when to continue.
B's short replies give B the power to end A's turns with approval.
B's readiness to pass the floor back gives B control over the rhythm.

A: A's floor-holding depends on B's willingness to listen, so B controls how long A speaks.
A's pace only matters if B accepts it, so B can slow the discussion down.
A decides when a point is complete, but B decides when it is accepted.
B: Acknowledging turn ends is a passive pattern that does not steer the flow.
B's replies are too short to end A's turns in any meaningful way.
Passing the floor back shows that B yields, which means A keeps control of the rhythm.

engagement.summary:
engagement of A: A invites reflection and works through the consequences, which draws B into the discussion.
engagement of B: B agrees with each point but adds no questions or personal experience.

A: A invites reflection on consequences, which shows A's investment in the topic.
A works through the implications, so A is the most engaged participant.
A's concern about getting people moving signals a stake in the outcome.
B: B's agreement shows attention to A's points, which makes B a receptive partner.
B's quick affirmations keep the discussion warm and give B a supportive presence.
B's endorsement can encourage A to keep developing the argument.

A: Inviting reflection is an open request that B can leave unanswered.
Working through implications is only effective if B engages with them, so B determines the depth.
A's concern is a stake that B can dismiss without changing the discussion.
B: Quick affirmations show attention but do not show investment in the topic.
Warmth without content does not give B much influence over the discussion.
Encouragement depends on A's willingness to continue, so A still drives the argument.
